title: General design of enzymes for new chemical reactions

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reliable way to turn a specified chemical reaction into an efficient, selective enzyme across a broad range of chemically different transformations. A researcher would specify the starting molecules, desired products and operating conditions, and the workflow would develop a protein catalyst with useful performance while keeping experimental screening within a defined budget. The ambition includes reactions without known enzymatic solutions; it does not require success for every conceivable reaction.

In the concept's scientific framing, this requires solving two connected design problems: identifying catalytic chemistry that can accelerate the desired transformation, and constructing a protein environment that makes that chemistry work. Arranging an established catalytic motif inside a new protein addresses an important part of the second problem. A broadly general workflow would also need to handle unfamiliar catalytic requirements, rather than depend entirely on arrangements already known to work. These distinctions describe the proposed capability; the supplied evidence does not establish that it has been achieved.

significance.text: If achieved, reliable reaction-to-enzyme design would make biocatalysis more programmable. Researchers could approach a new transformation through a reusable design workflow instead of beginning a large, bespoke laboratory evolution campaign each time. The direct advance would be greater predictability and broader access to selective catalysts, with experimental work serving validation and bounded refinement rather than an open-ended search. This is a conditional impact argument drawn from the proposed capability.

Cheaper manufacture of medicines and materials is a plausible downstream possibility, but an effective enzyme alone would not establish an economical process. Benefits would depend on feedstocks, enzyme production, operating conditions, competing reactions, product recovery and scale-up. The analogy to programming therefore has limits: specifying a desired reaction does not guarantee that a physically feasible catalyst exists, and a catalyst that works in a laboratory assay may still be unsuitable for manufacturing.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is dependable joint design of catalytic chemistry and a compatible protein across unfamiliar transformations. The research describes existing methods as insufficiently reliable for that goal, but the retained scientific evidence does not establish the extent of the limitation or its continuing scope. The substantive research question remains how to move from success on selected reaction families to a workflow whose performance transfers predictably across diverse chemistry.

The proposed problem involves several coupled physical requirements. A design must favor the desired reaction pathway and its transition states, position the relevant chemical groups, and accommodate protein motion and solvent effects. It must also suppress competing reactions sufficiently to deliver useful selectivity. A plausible static arrangement is therefore only part of the problem: the surrounding protein and reaction conditions must sustain productive chemistry. This is an explanatory synthesis of the supplied research framing, rather than a technical finding verified from the retained source.

A practical breakthrough would also require predicting which designs will work well enough to avoid extensive screening. Generality would be weakened if every unfamiliar reaction required expert invention of its catalytic arrangement or a large new evolution campaign. Conversely, some experimental refinement can fit the concept if its budget and role are defined in advance. The central engineering challenge is reliable performance with bounded iteration, alongside a clear account of where the workflow fails.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a paper as “Computational enzyme design by catalytic motif scaffolding,” attributes it to Markus Braun and colleagues, and gives a publication date of 3 December 2025 and DOI 10.1038/s41586-025-09747-9. It reports catalysts for two reaction classes, with some activities comparable to catalysts improved by laboratory evolution. These bibliographic and scientific details remain unverified here: according to the supplied review, the retained copy at the linked PubMed address contains only a cookie-related access message, without an abstract or article text. The link identifies the intended source, but the retained content cannot substantiate the reported results.

The research interprets that work as building protein scaffolds around established catalytic arrangements. If confirmed, this would demonstrate a narrower capability than general invention of active-site chemistry: successfully hosting a known catalytic arrangement does not by itself show that a workflow can discover suitable chemistry for unfamiliar reactions. Likewise, activity comparable to selected laboratory-evolved catalysts would require context about the reactions, assay conditions and comparison set before supporting a broader performance claim. Those details cannot be checked from the retained source.

The earlier research also refers to an accessible bibliographic record, a first-pass reading, and failed attempts to open the publisher page and PDF. The supplied review found no preserved material documenting those readings or access attempts, so they cannot serve as additional verification. The documented limitation is the cookie-only retained artifact. Missing article content does not show that the reported results are false, but it prevents a firm account of what was demonstrated. The supplied materials also do not establish comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026 or whether the broader capability remained open at that date.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: evaluate one workflow on a preregistered, independently selected panel of chemically diverse reactions, including transformations without known enzymatic solutions. Before testing, define reaction-specific activity and selectivity thresholds, the allowed experimental screening budget, and the panel success rate required for a convincing result. These would be proposed evaluation choices, not established standards. The panel should make clear which catalytic requirements are supplied to the workflow and which it must derive.
completion_criteria.label: Diverse reaction panel meets preregistered success thresholds within screening budget

completion_criteria.text: Independent laboratories should reproduce several successful designs under predefined, realistic conditions. Reports should document experimental iteration, failed designs and assay conditions so that apparent generality cannot be explained by unreported screening or unusually favorable comparisons. Performance should be judged against the intended use: a useful research catalyst and a useful manufacturing catalyst may face different requirements for activity, selectivity, stability and operating conditions. This is a proposed reproducibility and practicality framework.
completion_criteria.label: Independent laboratories reproduce successful designs under realistic, use-specific conditions

completion_criteria.text: A convincing outcome would establish demonstrated breadth within a stated chemical and operational domain. It should distinguish reuse of established catalytic motifs from cases in which the workflow derives unfamiliar catalytic arrangements, and identify reactions or conditions outside its reliable range. A finite panel cannot establish literal universality; its value is evidence that the same method transfers across meaningfully different challenges with a bounded experimental burden.
completion_criteria.label: Chemical and operational breadth is demonstrated with stated reliability limits

related_concepts.text: BCH-02, “Predict biochemical function from molecular sequence and environment,” overlaps through the need to connect protein sequence and operating conditions to catalytic behavior. The distinction is between prediction and construction: BCH-02 asks what a molecular system will do, while BCH-01 asks how to create a catalyst for a chosen transformation. Accurate prediction could support enzyme design without itself delivering a working design workflow. This comparison is a synthesis based on the supplied roster.

BCH-03, “A self-maintaining, evolvable cell assembled from defined components,” could benefit from designed enzymes that supply missing reactions, but cellular maintenance and evolution require coordinated systems beyond an individual catalyst. BCH-04, “A chemically plausible route from simple feedstocks to evolving heredity,” concerns the emergence of heredity; deliberately engineered enzymes would not by themselves establish a chemically plausible origin pathway. BCH-07, “Autonomous heredity in a chemically distinct genetic polymer,” could intersect with enzymes that synthesize or process alternative polymers, while autonomous information inheritance remains a separate achievement. These are conceptual relationships inferred from the roster.

BCH-08, “Resolve the nitrogenase reaction cycle during nitrogen fixation,” shares the challenge of understanding catalytic chemistry. Resolving that particular mechanism could inform catalyst design, but mechanistic understanding of one enzyme and general design across reaction classes are distinct goals. BCH-09, “Predict and control the biochemical organization of condensates,” and BCH-10, “Predict modification-dependent biochemical networks,” concern environmental organization and interacting biochemical processes that could affect a designed enzyme's behavior. Success in an isolated reaction would not establish control over those larger systems. This is a roster-based comparison.

BCH-05, “Routine, comprehensive single-cell proteoform reading,” BCH-06, “A multiplexed biochemical flight recorder for living cells,” and BCH-11, “Routine structural reading of complex glycans,” concern measurement capabilities that could help characterize enzymes, cellular responses or reaction products in relevant applications. Their core achievements remain distinct: reading protein variants, recording cellular events and resolving glycan structures do not themselves provide a general route to designing catalytic chemistry. These possible connections are synthesis rather than demonstrated dependencies.

brief.title: Custom proteins for new chemical reactions
possible: A researcher could specify starting molecules, desired products and working conditions, then obtain an enzyme—a protein that speeds up a chemical reaction. The same workflow could serve many different reactions, including ones without a known enzyme solution, within a fixed budget for laboratory testing.
why: Researchers could develop useful enzymes through a repeatable process instead of starting a lengthy laboratory search for each reaction. More predictable design would give chemists broader access to proteins that make the desired product while limiting unwanted reactions.

sources.showed: They built new proteins around established arrangements of chemical groups that drive reactions. The proteins handled different reaction types, with activities rivalling enzymes improved through laboratory mutation and selection.
sources.quote: High-resolution structures of six of the designs revealed near-atomic active site design precision.
sources.cited_for: Established catalytic arrangements can work efficiently inside newly designed proteins.
sources.not_established: This does not show that a workflow can discover suitable catalytic chemistry for unfamiliar reactions.

sources.who: Donghyo Kim, Seth M. Woodbury, Woody Ahern and colleagues
sources.showed: They designed proteins that use zinc to help water break a chemical bond. The most active protein closely matched its predicted structure, without experimental optimization.
sources.quote:
the crystal structure of 
the most active design is very close to the design model, demonstrating the accuracy 
of the design method.
sources.cited_for: Proteins built around a calculated chemical arrangement can achieve high activity.
sources.not_established: Success on the tested reaction does not establish reliable design across diverse chemistry.

sources.showed: They designed efficient proteins for a model reaction without repeated rounds of mutation and laboratory screening. Their workflow assembled structural fragments from natural proteins.
sources.quote: designs exhibit efficiencies greater than 2,000 M−1 s−1.
sources.cited_for: Efficient enzymes can emerge from computational design with limited experimental testing.
sources.not_established: A successful model reaction does not establish transfer to unfamiliar reaction families.

sources.showed: They designed enzymes that join molecules while favouring a particular product shape. Changing the binding region changed which starting molecules the enzymes could use.
sources.quote: X-ray crystallography confirms that the structure matches the design for the most active of the enzymes, and binding site substitutions reprogram the substrate specificity.
sources.cited_for: Computational design can create proteins that accelerate selective bond-forming reactions.
sources.not_established: Selected working designs do not demonstrate a dependable workflow across chemically diverse reactions.

sources.showed: They improved existing artificial enzymes by designing around multiple protein shapes inferred from X-ray measurements. This reduced reliance on repeated laboratory mutation and screening.
sources.quote:
The most active design displays a
catalytic efficiency improved by approximately 250-fold
sources.cited_for: Accounting for protein flexibility can improve enzyme design.
sources.not_established: Improving existing enzymes for a model reaction does not demonstrate design from an unfamiliar reaction alone.

shown: Braun and colleagues built efficient proteins around established reaction-driving arrangements. Kim and colleagues built active zinc-containing enzymes around arrangements calculated from chemistry. Both demonstrate progress in making a protein support specified chemistry.

Listov and colleagues designed efficient enzymes for a model reaction with limited laboratory testing. Rakotoharisoa and colleagues improved artificial enzymes by accounting for their changing shapes. These successes cover selected reactions.
missing: A dependable workflow still needs to design both unfamiliar reaction-driving chemistry and a protein that makes it work.
The same workflow must meet predefined activity and product-selectivity targets across diverse reactions within a fixed testing budget.
Independent laboratories must reproduce successful designs under conditions suited to their intended uses.
The workflow must establish where it works reliably and where it fails.

milestones.label: Diverse reactions succeed within a fixed testing budget
milestones.explanation: One workflow would have to meet advance-set targets on an independently chosen, chemically diverse panel, including reactions without known enzyme solutions. This would test breadth without open-ended laboratory searching.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce useful performance
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce several designs under realistic, predefined conditions, reporting failures and experimental iteration. This would establish whether performance transfers to intended uses.

milestones.label: Reliable breadth and its limits become clear
milestones.explanation: Results would have to establish reliable chemical and operating ranges, distinguishing reused catalytic arrangements from newly derived ones. This would show where the method transfers and where it fails.

uncertain: How much unfamiliar catalytic chemistry can a workflow derive rather than receive from an expert?
Which reaction panel, performance targets and testing budget would make a convincing demonstration?
How reliably will laboratory activity translate into performance under intended working conditions?

page.title: De novo enzyme design for user-defined reactions
page.definition: The user specifies the starting molecule or molecules, the desired product and the required activity and product selectivity. Across reactions with different mechanisms, the workflow chooses the arrangement of chemical groups that carries out each reaction and designs a protein sequence that holds those groups in place. It can use known protein folds even when no natural enzyme is known to catalyse the requested reaction.

goal.need: Drug manufacturers can lose product during purification when a reaction makes a mixture of stereoisomers. In sitagliptin manufacture, an evolved enzyme eliminated a purification step and cut total waste by 19%. Designing an enzyme for the intended product would let chemists pursue similarly selective routes even when no natural catalyst is known for a step or the reaction is difficult to screen at scale. The enzyme must still work under process conditions, including in any solvent needed to dissolve the starting material.

completion.title: One workflow exceeds 50% success at designing enzymes with kcat/KM >10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ across mechanisms.
completion.criterion: For user-specified reactions with different catalytic mechanisms, including one without a known natural enzyme, one workflow determines catalytic-group arrangements and protein sequences. For each reaction, more than 50% of experimentally tested designs must achieve catalytic efficiency kcat/KM >10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ and satisfy product-selectivity targets under assay conditions fixed before design. At least one mechanism must lie outside the workflow's development set.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback combining EBRC's separately published activity and success-rate targets with prospective testing across reaction mechanisms.
completion.basis: Searched EBRC's 2019 and 2020 roadmaps, NSF's USPRD solicitation, AME, and enzyme-design benchmark and prize literature. Found separate activity and success-rate targets, but no joint experimental acceptance test for reaction-to-enzyme generality. This Atlas test combines EBRC's numerical targets with prospective selectivity and transfer to a mechanism outside the development set.

milestones.title: A designed protein accelerates its target reaction and is regenerated during catalysis.
milestones.criterion: The designed protein increases the rate of the specified reaction relative to the same reaction without the protein and is regenerated during the catalytic cycle.
milestones.set_by: IUPAC, definition of catalyst in its 1994 physical-organic-chemistry terminology recommendations.
milestones.threshold_quote: increases its rate but without a net change in the amount of that substance in the system.

milestones.title: A designed protein model passes AME's 1.5 Å active-site test with zero ligand clashes.
milestones.criterion: For at least one of eight LigandMPNN sequences assigned to a designed backbone, align the Chai-1 prediction to the reference motif on the N, Cα and C atoms of the catalytic residues. The root-mean-square deviation over all heavy atoms of those residues must be <1.5 Å, and the same prediction must have no protein atom within 1.5 Å of a ligand atom.
milestones.set_by: Ahern et al., published atomic motif enzyme (AME) computational benchmark protocol.
milestones.threshold_quote: the design contains no clashes with the ligand where a clash is defined as two atoms being within 1.5 Å.

milestones.title: A computationally designed enzyme exceeds 10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ in catalytic efficiency.
milestones.criterion: Before directed evolution, a computationally designed enzyme has an experimentally measured catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) greater than 10⁵ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ for its specified substrate and reaction.
milestones.set_by: Natural-enzyme catalytic-efficiency benchmark used in EBRC's 2019 roadmap and Listov et al.'s 2025 experimental comparison. This milestone applies the numerical benchmark to an individual enzyme.
milestones.threshold_quote: Routine design of enzymes with high activities (i.e., k_{cat}/K_{M} > 10^{5} 1/M*s).

milestones.title: A designed enzyme preferentially forms the specified stereoisomer.
milestones.criterion: For a reaction with competing stereoisomeric products, specify the target stereoisomer before design. Resolve the products experimentally and compare their distribution with the uncatalysed reaction. The enzyme must favour formation of the target over its specified competitor and increase the target-to-competitor ratio above background.
milestones.set_by: IUPAC defines stereoselectivity. Siegel and colleagues apply it to a specified design target by measuring the catalysed and background product distributions.
milestones.threshold_quote: The preferential formation in a chemical reaction of one stereoisomer over another.

milestones.title: More than 50% of designs tested for one target reaction show catalytic activity.
milestones.criterion: For one specified reaction, report the number of distinct designs tested experimentally and the number that show activity on the target substrate above the negative control. The number active divided by the total number tested must exceed 0.50.
milestones.set_by: EBRC's 2019 Biomolecular Engineering roadmap supplies the percentage. The activity screen used by Braun and colleagues defines a hit for this single-reaction milestone.
milestones.threshold_quote: A rate of success greater than 50% would therefore have a tremendous impact.

not_found: No externally specified reaction panel, numerical product-selectivity requirement or experimental screening budget for general reaction-to-enzyme design was found.
No published definition was found for the number or diversity of reaction mechanisms required to establish generality.
No academy, professional society or roadmap statement was found disputing the feasibility or value of designing enzymes for user-defined reactions.

definition = "The user specifies the starting molecule or molecules, the desired product and the required activity and product selectivity. Across reactions with different mechanisms, the workflow chooses the arrangement of chemical groups that carries out each reaction and designs a protein sequence that holds those groups in place. It can use known protein folds even when no natural enzyme is known to catalyse the requested reaction.". Reason: The definition leaves unclear what the user supplies, what the workflow must design and whether it may use an existing protein fold.

goal.need = "Drug manufacturers can lose product during purification when a reaction makes a mixture of stereoisomers. In sitagliptin manufacture, an evolved enzyme eliminated a purification step and cut total waste by 19%. Designing an enzyme for the intended product would let chemists pursue similarly selective routes even when no natural catalyst is known for a step or the reaction is difficult to screen at scale. The enzyme must still work under process conditions, including in any solvent needed to dissolve the starting material.". Reason: The current rationale counts variants in a model reaction but omits the manufacturing problem, its measured cost in waste and the conditions for a useful enzyme.

add statement by Engineering Biology Research Consortium, 2019: "values of natural enzymes for artificial (user-defined) reactions.". Reason: The existing 2019 quotation gives a success rate but omits the roadmap's explicit goal for the reactions users choose.

add not found: "No academy, professional society or roadmap statement was found disputing the feasibility or value of designing enzymes for user-defined reactions.". Reason: The search for a formal objection to the goal yielded no statement from a body with standing.

edit m1: criterion = "The designed protein increases the rate of the specified reaction relative to the same reaction without the protein and is regenerated during the catalytic cycle."; refs = [7]. Reason: The criterion mixes the IUPAC test for catalysis with the outcomes of two design campaigns.

edit m2: criterion = "For at least one of eight LigandMPNN sequences assigned to a designed backbone, align the Chai-1 prediction to the reference motif on the N, C\u03b1 and C atoms of the catalytic residues. The root-mean-square deviation over all heavy atoms of those residues must be <1.5 \u00c5, and the same prediction must have no protein atom within 1.5 \u00c5 of a ligand atom."; refs = [6]. Reason: The criterion mixes the AME computational test with published results, including a crystal-structure comparison that uses a different set of atoms.

edit m3: criterion = "Before directed evolution, a computationally designed enzyme has an experimentally measured catalytic efficiency (kcat/KM) greater than 10\u2075 M\u207b\u00b9 s\u207b\u00b9 for its specified substrate and reaction."; refs = [5, 10]. Reason: The efficiency criterion includes results and replicate counts from individual experiments that are unnecessary for stating the threshold.

add milestone after m2: "A designed enzyme preferentially forms the specified stereoisomer.". Reason: Neither detectable activity nor high catalytic efficiency establishes that a designed enzyme favours the intended stereoisomer.

add milestone after m3: "More than 50% of designs tested for one target reaction show catalytic activity.". Reason: The existing milestones measure individual proteins and leave the experimental success rate of a design campaign untested until completion.
